Field surveys of the Kor River chub (Alburnoides qanati) in its type locality have provided detailed morphometric data for this endemic cyprinid. The species attains an ultimate total length of 11.9 centimeters [Li = 11.9 centimeters], a modest size consistent with other members of the genus inhabiting mountainous streams of the Middle East. Specimens collected during the breeding season revealed that the total length at which individuals first exhibit mature gonadal tissue is 3 centimeters [Lp = 3 centimeters], indicating a relatively early onset of pubertal development compared to several congeners from larger river systems. This size at maturation suggests that reproductive investment begins well before somatic growth is complete, a pattern frequently observed in small-bodied cyprinids inhabiting unpredictable lotic environments where early reproduction may buffer against sporadic recruitment success.

Reproductive output in Alburnoides qanati has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions reflecting the thermal regime of its native habitat. When maintained at a constant water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], females produce a maximum of approximately 2368 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2368 eggs per year], with each spawning event yielding approximately six eggs and roughly ten spawning events occurring throughout an extended breeding season. This iteroparous strategy, combining moderate fecundity per event with a high annual frequency of reproductive episodes, is interpreted as an adaptation to the patchy and seasonal availability of suitable spawning substrates in the gravel beds of the Kor River. The total annual reproductive effort derived from these values is substantial for a fish of this body size.

The early life stages of the Kor River chub are characterized by rapid development under local thermal conditions. At the same experimental temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the embryonic period is brief, with age at hatching occurring just 13 days after fertilization [ab = 13 days after fertilization]. Hatchlings emerge as yolk-sac larvae that are entirely lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous reserves during the first days post-eclosion. The wet weight of the newly emerged larva at the moment of hatching is approximately 0.00017 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00017 grams], a mass that reflects the small egg diameter of about 0.69 millimeters. This minimal initial mass necessitates rapid yolk absorption and a swift transition to exogenous feeding to fuel subsequent growth through the larval and juvenile phases.

As individuals progress toward adulthood, distinct shifts in body mass mark the transition from the immature to the mature state. The wet weight at which the typical Alburnoides qanati individual attains puberty is 0.25 grams [Wwp = 0.25 grams], corresponding closely with the aforementioned length of 3 centimeters and signalling the completion of the juvenile growth phase. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults in the population reaches 24.26 grams [Wwi = 24.26 grams], indicating an approximately hundred-fold increase in somatic mass from the pubertal stage. This substantial post-pubertal growth trajectory is characteristic of species that allocate resources to both continued body enlargement and reproductive effort throughout their adult lives, a life-history strategy common among iteroparous freshwater teleosts.

Longevity data for this species, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith analysis, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5,475 days [am = approximately 5,475 days] at the prevailing water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C] in the Kor River system, which translates to roughly 15 years. This relatively extended lifespan for a cyprinid of such modest size suggests a life-history strategy emphasizing adult survival and repeated reproductive events over many seasons. The combination of early maturation at 3 centimeters, a high annual reproductive output facilitated by multiple spawning events, and a long potential reproductive lifespan positions Alburnoides qanati as a species well-suited to the environmental variability of its arid-zone river habitat, where protracted adult survival can buffer against years of poor recruitment.
